reading.body:
Three large drugmakers have signed company-wide agreements with frontier AI labs rather than buying narrow tools. Sanofi partnered with OpenAI and Formation Bio in 2024, Novo Nordisk announced a partnership with OpenAI in April 2026, and Bristol Myers Squibb announced an agreement with Anthropic to bring Claude across the company.

The pattern is consolidation at the top of the buyer. Each deal is framed as spanning the whole enterprise, not a single function: Novo Nordisk covers discovery, trials and production planning, and the BMS agreement positions Claude across the business. That is a different purchase from a point tool for one team. It routes a large share of a company's AI usage through one vendor's models, roadmap and pricing.

For AI specifically, the constraint this addresses is not compute or power but integration and governance. A single primary partner simplifies procurement, security review and training, which is why regulated companies with heavy review burdens gravitate to it. The stated trade off is dependence, and the stated mitigation is portability: model-neutral integration layers and evaluation of other models for specific tasks.

What the data does not cover is scale. There are no contract values, no user counts, no deployment timelines, and no results. It names three companies, which is a signal about the largest pharma buyers and not about the industry as a whole. It also says nothing about how these agreements interact with the compute and power those models ultimately run on.

The three deals differ in what they actually cover. Sanofi's 2024 collaboration with OpenAI and Formation Bio is scoped to building AI tools for drug development, a joint build. Novo Nordisk's April 2026 partnership spans discovery, trials and production planning, which reaches into operations rather than only research. The BMS agreement with Anthropic is the broadest in framing, positioning Claude across the business. A reader comparing them is comparing three different depths of commitment, not three instances of the same deal.

The vendor split matters. Two of the three named companies chose OpenAI and one chose Anthropic, so there is no single lab consolidating pharma. The consolidation the data supports is at the buyer, where one lab becomes the primary partner, not at the supplier, where the field remains divided. That distinction changes the lock-in question: a drugmaker's dependence runs to one vendor's roadmap, but the market still offers a credible second option to evaluate against it.

The dates also carry information. Sanofi signed in May 2024, Novo Nordisk in April 2026, BMS in 2026. The gap is roughly two years, and the later two arrive within the same year. Whatever the cause, the data shows the pace of these announcements accelerating rather than a steady trickle, and it shows the first mover was a research collaboration while the later two are enterprise-wide.

Why would a drugmaker sign one company-wide deal instead of buying tools team by team?

The data gives the stated reason rather than a measured one: broad access to leading models, early capabilities, joint development support, and help with deployment. It does not contain cost comparisons, procurement timelines, or evidence that the enterprise deal outperforms point tools. The case for consolidation in this data is a governance and access argument, not a results argument.

What does Novo Nordisk's partnership with OpenAI actually cover?

Discovery, trials and production planning, announced 14 April 2026. That is the widest functional scope of the three deals in the data. No contract value, user count, or deployment timeline is given.

Is Bristol Myers Squibb using OpenAI or Anthropic?

Anthropic. The agreement positions Claude across the business, announced in 2026. The data does not say which models BMS uses elsewhere or whether the agreement is exclusive.

How do these companies avoid depending on a single vendor?

The stated mitigation is portability: keep data and workflows portable, use integration layers that can switch models, and evaluate other models for specific tasks. The data does not name any integration layer, vendor, or standard, and does not say whether any of the three companies has actually done this.

Did these partnerships produce any results?

The data holds no outcomes. There are no trial accelerations, cost figures, headcount changes, or deployment milestones attached to any of the three agreements. Anything about what the deals delivered is outside this data.

How many pharma companies have signed deals like these?

The data names three: Sanofi, Novo Nordisk and Bristol Myers Squibb. It does not give a count for the industry, so it cannot say whether three is most of the large buyers or a small sample.

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Frontier AI labs build the most capable general models. Drugmakers sign strategic agreements with them for broad access across the company, early access to new capabilities, joint development of tools for research or operations, and support with deployment. Several of the largest pharma companies now have such agreements, often with one lab as a primary partner.

A single primary partner simplifies procurement, security review and training. The trade off is dependence on one vendor's roadmap, pricing and policies. Many companies therefore keep critical workflows portable, use model neutral integration layers, and evaluate other models for specific tasks.

What the partnerships are

Since 2023, most large pharmaceutical companies have announced relationships with the companies that build the largest AI models. The shapes vary: enterprise licences for a model with privacy guarantees, joint teams building specific applications, access to models before public release, dedicated computing capacity, and in a few cases equity investments or revenue sharing on drugs discovered together. Some pair with one lab; others deliberately work with several to avoid dependence.

What each side wants

Pharma companies want capability they cannot build, early access to improvements, and a partner that will adapt a model to regulated work rather than sell a consumer product. The labs want proprietary scientific data, hard problems that prove their models, and revenue from a sector with deep budgets. The best known results so far are in drug discovery, medical writing and document heavy work; the most ambitious claims, about models designing medicines end to end, are still being tested in trials.

What to look for in the agreements

The durable questions are about data and control. Does the pharma company's data train the lab's models, and if so, who owns what is learned? Can the company inspect the model well enough to validate its use in regulated processes? What happens when the lab retires or changes a model the company has built around? And how is intellectual property shared when a model contributes to a discovery? Companies that answer those questions in the contract, rather than in a dispute later, get the most from the relationship.
